Based on the search results, I found several relevant discussions about the `xcodebuild exportArchive` "Cloud signing permission error" and "No profiles were found" issues related to App Store Connect API keys.

## Key Issues & Solutions:

### Cloud Signing Permission Error

Distribution signing with cloud signing options requires an App Store Connect API key with Admin-level access, and using a non-admin API key results in the error "Cloud signing permission error".

**Solution:** The only way for the command to succeed is through the use of an API key with Admin access. However, enabling "Access to Cloud Managed Distribution Certificate" in App Store Connect → Users and Access for your account can help resolve the issue.

### "No profiles were found" Error

The error "No profiles for '<bundle_id>' were found" occurs when Xcode couldn't find any iOS App Store provisioning profiles matching the bundle ID. This can be resolved by enabling "Access to Cloud Managed Distribution Certificate" in App Store Connect, as Xcode 13 may fail to recognize locally installed distribution certificates and attempt to use cloud signing.

### Backend Permission Issues

Apple confirmed that the root cause can be an App Store Connect API–related permission issue that requires a backend update on their side. If you encounter a 403 Forbidden error or ResultCode 7495, contacting Apple Developer Technical Support with IDEDistributionProvisioning logs is recommended.

### Command Usage

With Xcode 13, you can use cloud signing by using the `-allowProvisioningUpdates` flag along with the App Store API key instead of a developer ID logged into Xcode.

Cloud signing (creating the App Store *distribution* certificate and the missing `dev.malpercio.identitywallet` profile on the fly) requires an **Admin** key. I told you to make an **App Manager** key — and an App Manager key produces *exactly* this `Cloud signing permission error`. **Fix (~2 min, no project changes):**

   mv ~/Downloads/AuthKey_<NEWKEYID>.p8 ~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/

   export APPLE_API_KEY=<new key id>
   export APPLE_API_KEY_PATH=~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/AuthKey_<NEWKEYID>.p8
   export APPLE_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=<team id>
   ```
3. Re-run `just ios-ipa`. With an Admin key, xcodebuild's `-allowProvisioningUpdates` creates the missing App Store profile automatically and the export completes.

- Update the **GitHub secrets** (`APPLE_API_KEY` + `APPLE_API_KEY_B64`) to the new Admin key — **CI runs the same cloud signing and will fail identically with an App Manager key.**
- Alternative if you'd rather not use an Admin key: enable **"Access to Cloud Managed Distribution Certificate"** under Users and Access for the key's user — but the Admin key is the clean, CI-matching path.

  distribution cert + provisioning profile on the fly, which an App Manager key can't

  `APPLE_API_KEY_B64`. (Locally, also ensure the `APPLE_API_*` vars are exported before
  `just ios-ipa` — without them xcodebuild has no credential to create the profile.)

content.text:
Done — runbook and memory both corrected (role → **Admin**, plus a troubleshooting entry for this exact error so it doesn't bite again).

To recap the path forward: regenerate the Team Key as **Admin** → drop the new `.p8` in `~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/` and `export` the four `APPLE_API_*` vars → re-run `just ios-ipa` (the export should now create the profile and succeed) → then push the **same Admin key** into the GitHub secrets so CI matches. That was the last credential gap; the build itself already works, so once the export signs you've got a green local run and you're clear to push.

Sources that confirmed the Admin requirement:
- [Why does xcodebuild require admin — Apple Developer Forums](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/698117)
- [Cloud signing permission error — Apple Developer Forums](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/810658)
- [Role permissions — App Store Connect Help](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/account-management/role-permissions/)

Massive progress in there — read past the wall of build settings and you can see: **the Rust compiled, the app linked, the archive exported, and `Obsign.ipa` was produced.** Two distinct problems remain, and I spotted a bug of mine in the logs:

1. **Signing cert is a Tauri placeholder.** Look at the export step: `found cert "Apple Distribution: Tauri (unset)"` → `Signing with identity "Apple Distribution: Tauri (unset)"`. That's **not** a real Apple Distribution certificate for your team (`6U6Y3HQ9DH`) — it's a dummy Tauri generates as a fallback. App Store Connect then rejects it: *"Invalid Provisioning Profile … Missing code-signing certificate."*
2. **My `ios-upload` recipe grabbed the wrong file.** It says `uploading …/Identity Wallet.ipa` — a **stale pre-rename artifact**. The build made `Obsign.ipa`, but my recipe globbed `*.ipa` and the array picks alphabetically, so `Identity Wallet.ipa` (leftover from before the rename) won out. That's a real bug — it should pick the newest.

The signing one is the substantive blocker, and it's a known Tauri-iOS rough edge, so let me verify the exact fix rather than guess.

## iOS Code Signing for App Store Distribution

To distribute iOS applications you must have your bundle identifier registered in the App Store Connect, an appropriate iOS code signing certificate and a mobile provisioning profile that links them together and enables the iOS capabilities used by your app.

For App Store distribution, the provisioning profile must be an "App Store Connect" profile, and you should select the appropriate App ID and link the certificate you previously created.

## Manual Certificate Configuration

For manual signing (rather than letting Xcode manage it automatically), you need to navigate to the Certificates page to create a new Apple Distribution certificate, download the new certificate and install it to the macOS Keychain.

For App Store distribution, it must be an "App Store Connect" profile, and you should select the appropriate App ID and link the certificate you previously created.

The search results provide comprehensive documentation on the proper setup process for iOS code signing with Tauri, including details about certificate creation, provisioning profile setup, and environment variable configuration for the build process.

Verified — and this is a **known Tauri v2 rough edge**, not something you're doing wrong. Tauri's *automatic* iOS App Store signing is buggy ([tauri#11092 "Export method does not work"](https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/issues/11092)): when you give it only an API key, it falls back to a self-signed **"Apple Distribution: Tauri (unset)"** placeholder, which App Store Connect rejects. The reliable fix the community uses is **explicit signing** — give Tauri a real distribution certificate + an App Store provisioning profile via env vars.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **The API key was the wrong tool for the *signing* half.** It's perfect for the *upload* (altool), but Tauri's iOS export won't reliably cloud-create a distribution cert — so we provide one. The upside: this **converges your local and CI signing** onto the exact same mechanism (3 base64 env vars), which is what CI needs anyway (no Xcode GUI on a runner). So this isn't a detour — it's the CI path, validated locally first.
- **My original "no certs to manage" pitch was too optimistic for Tauri iOS.** That's on me; the design adjusts to explicit cert+profile.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

      *":${_ezpds_shim}:"*) : ;;
      *) export PATH="${_ezpds_shim}:${PATH}" ;;
    esac
    unset _ezpds_shim
  fi
fi

content.text: The grep was misleading me — reading the real YAML, `buildPhase: resources` actually belongs to the `assets` entry (the web frontend, correct). `Externals` (line 33) has **no** explicit buildPhase, so XcodeGen *infers* `resources` for the `.a` files. So the durable fix is `buildPhase: none` on `Externals` in `project.yml` (the source the build syncs from) **plus** stripping the live pbxproj — belt and suspenders, so it can't come back on a re-sync. Let me upgrade Patch F to cover both layers.

input.old_string:
# --- Patch F: don't ship the Rust staticlib inside the .app (App Store rejects it) ---
# cargo-mobile2 adds `libapp.a` to BOTH the Frameworks phase (correct — it is linked via
# `-lapp`) AND the Copy Bundle Resources phase (wrong — a standalone `.a` inside the .app
# is rejected on upload: "libapp.a ... is not permitted / Invalid bundle structure",
# tauri#13578). Strip ONLY the Resources entries; the build-file/file IDs are random per
# `cargo tauri ios init`, so match cargo-mobile2's stable comment `libapp.a in Resources`.
# The `libapp.a in Frameworks` (link) entry is left intact. Idempotent: a re-run finds none.
if grep -q 'libapp\.a in Resources' "${PBXPROJ}"; then
  /usr/bin/perl -ni -e 'print unless m{/\* libapp\.a in Resources \*/}' "${PBXPROJ}"
  if grep -q 'libapp\.a in Resources' "${PBXPROJ}"; then
    echo "error: could not strip 'libapp.a in Resources' from the pbxproj (Patch F)." >&2
    echo "       cargo-mobile2's template may differ; inspect the Copy Bundle Resources" >&2
    echo "       phase in ${PBXPROJ} and adjust the regex in $(basename "$0")." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  echo "ios-postinit: stripped libapp.a from Copy Bundle Resources (App Store bundle fix)"
else
  echo "ios-postinit: libapp.a already absent from Resources phase"
fi

# .app — which App Store upload rejects ("libapp.a ... is not permitted / Invalid bundle
# structure", tauri#13578). The staticlib is still LINKED via the separate `framework:
# libapp.a` entry + LIBRARY_SEARCH_PATHS, so keeping it out of resources is safe. Fix at
# both layers: project.yml (the source the build re-syncs from) and the live pbxproj.
PROJYML="$(dirname "${PBXPROJ}")/../project.yml"
if [ -f "${PROJYML}" ]; then
  if grep -A1 -E '^[[:space:]]*-[[:space:]]*path:[[:space:]]*Externals[[:space:]]*$' "${PROJYML}" | grep -q 'buildPhase: none'; then

    /usr/bin/perl -0pi -e 's/^([ \t]*)- path: Externals[ \t]*\n/$1- path: Externals\n$1  buildPhase: none\n/m' "${PROJYML}"
    echo "ios-postinit: set project.yml Externals buildPhase:none (keeps libapp.a out of the bundle)"

fi
# Strip the already-generated `libapp.a in Resources` entries from the live pbxproj (IDs are

  if grep -q 'libapp\.a in Resources' "${PBXPROJ}"; then

459

462	Host builds (`cargo test` / `cargo build`) link fine because **rustc** does the final link and honors the crate's `#[link(name = "SystemConfiguration", kind = "framework")]`. ### `libapp.a ... is not permitted` / `Invalid bundle structure` on TestFlight upload

`cargo tauri ios build` succeeds and `xcrun altool` then rejects the upload (HTTP 409): *"The 'Obsign.app/libapp.a' binary file is not permitted. Your app cannot contain standalone executables or libraries."* (tauri#13578.)

cargo-mobile2 lists the `Externals` directory (which holds the Rust staticlib `libapp.a`) as a project source with **no explicit `buildPhase`**, so XcodeGen infers `resources` and copies the raw `.a` into the `.app` — which App Store validation forbids. The library is also (correctly) **linked** via the separate `framework: libapp.a` entry + `LIBRARY_SEARCH_PATHS`, so excluding it from resources is safe.

**Fix:** Already resolved automatically. `just ios-postinit` (Patch F) sets `Externals → buildPhase: none` in `gen/apple/project.yml` (the source the per-build sync regenerates from) **and** strips the `libapp.a in Resources` entry from the generated `project.pbxproj` (the `in Frameworks` link entry is kept). `just ios-check` verifies both.

---

### `base64: invalid option -- 'o'` during `cargo tauri ios build` signing

The build reads `IOS_CERTIFICATE` and fails decoding it: `base64: invalid option -- 'o'`. In the Nix dev shell, GNU coreutils `base64` shadows macOS's BSD `base64` in `PATH`, but Tauri's cert decode uses BSD-only flags (`-i`/`-o`). (CI is unaffected — the runner has no Nix.)

**Fix:** Already resolved automatically. `scripts/ios-env.sh` (under `EZPDS_IOS_BUILD=1`) shims `/usr/bin/base64` ahead of the Nix one via a tiny symlink dir on `PATH` — surgical (only `base64`), leaving every other Nix tool untouched.

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack**, trace backward:
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use ed3d-plan-and-execute:test-driven-development for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultrathink this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Integration with Other Skills

**This skill requires using:**

input.old_string:
# cargo-mobile2 uses xcodegen to generate the Xcode project. It isn't pre-installed,
      # and the Tauri CLI runs x86_64 (Rosetta) on the arm64 runner, so its own

input.new_string:
# The Tauri CLI runs x86_64 (Rosetta) on the arm64 runner, so every `brew` it shells
      # out to (cargo-mobile2 installs xcodegen, libimobiledevice, ios-deploy, ...) is
      # refused: "Cannot install under Rosetta 2 in ARM default prefix". Shim `brew` to
      # always re-exec under arm64 — fixes all of cargo-mobile2's brew calls at once,
      # rather than pre-installing each dep (tauri#11244, cargo-mobile2#291).
      - name: Force Homebrew under arm64 (Tauri CLI runs under Rosetta)
        run: |
          mkdir -p "$RUNNER_TEMP/arm64-shims"
          printf '#!/bin/bash\nexec arch -arm64 /opt/homebrew/bin/brew "$@"\n' > "$RUNNER_TEMP/arm64-shims/brew"
          chmod +x "$RUNNER_TEMP/arm64-shims/brew"
          echo "$RUNNER_TEMP/arm64-shims" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"

content.text:
Verified and committed (`7539c39`). The brew shim is the **general** fix — it routes *every* brew call cargo-mobile2 makes (xcodegen, libimobiledevice, ios-deploy, whatever else) through arm64, so the whole `init` step should clear in one shot rather than dying on the next dependency.

```bash
git push origin main
```

Then the usual: `gh run watch` → paste the result. The Rosetta/brew class is now solved at the root, so `cargo tauri ios init` should complete; if anything else turns red it'll be a *different* category (and the first time `ios-postinit` → build → sign → upload runs in the cloud), which we'll handle the same way.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **This is the moment the debugging shifted from symptom to root.** Two brew errors (xcodegen, libimobiledevice) were the same underlying fact — an x86_64 process can't drive `/opt/homebrew` — wearing different masks. Pre-installing each dep would've been an endless game; shimming `brew` to re-exec under arm64 fixes the *category*. When the same failure reappears in a new spot, that's the signal to stop patching instances and neutralize the cause.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**So close — and look how far it got:** CI ran the *entire* build and **signed the IPA in the cloud** (`Obsign.ipa` exists, altool is uploading it). Every hard part worked headless — `init`, the six patches, the Rosetta/brew fixes, the cert+profile signing. The only thing that failed is the **upload's authentication**, and your hunch is right — it's a secret.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **The error fingerprints *which* secrets are wrong.** `Failure to authenticate (-26000 / -1011)` is App Store Connect **API-key** auth — used *only* by the `altool` upload. The build **signed successfully**, which means your `IOS_CERTIFICATE` / `IOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` / `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION` secrets are *correct* (a bad cert would've failed the export, like your local "requires a provisioning profile" did). So the culprit is narrowed to exactly three: **`APPLE_API_KEY`, `APPLE_API_ISSUER`, `APPLE_API_KEY_B64`** — almost certainly set from a shell where the env vars weren't live (the same "exports don't persist" trap that bit you locally).
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Fix — re-set those three from known-good values** (your build log shows them exactly: Key ID `K49MN465ZW`, Issuer `69a6de84-cd9b-47e3-e053-5b8c7c11a4d1`):

```bash
# sanity-check the key file first:
head -1 ~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/AuthKey_K49MN465ZW.p8   # -> -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----

R=<you>/ezpds
gh secret set -R "$R" APPLE_API_KEY     -b "K49MN465ZW"
gh secret set -R "$R" APPLE_API_ISSUER  -b "69a6de84-cd9b-47e3-e053-5b8c7c11a4d1"
gh secret set -R "$R" APPLE_API_KEY_B64 -b "$(base64 -i ~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/AuthKey_K49MN465ZW.p8)"
```

(The `APPLE_API_KEY_B64` blob is the most error-prone — set it straight from the file like above, not from an env var that may have been empty.)

**Then re-run — no commit needed** (secrets are read at run time):
```bash
gh run rerun <run-id>     # or the Actions UI → the failed run → "Re-run failed jobs"
```
A full re-run rebuilds (~10 min) since it's one job, but it'll sign and this time **authenticate** the upload. If it *still* says "Failure to authenticate" after a clean re-set, that points at the key itself (revoked, or missing the **App Manager** role) rather than the secret plumbing — and I'll add a non-leaking secret-validation step to pinpoint it. But a re-set is the high-confidence fix here.

Authentication's fixed — the re-set worked. Now it's purely a toolchain-version gate: **the `macos-15` runner has Xcode 16.4 (iOS 18.5 SDK), but Apple now requires the iOS 26 SDK / Xcode 26+** to upload. Your *local* Mac is on Xcode 26.3 (the build logs showed `iPhoneOS26.2.sdk`), which is exactly why local uploads worked and the runner doesn't. The fix is a runner image with Xcode 26. - **Patch F** (`ios-postinit.sh` + `ios-check.sh` guard): cargo-mobile2 copies the Rust staticlib `libapp.a` into the `.app`; App Store rejects loose libs (tauri#13578). Patch F sets `Externals → buildPhase: none` in `project.yml` AND strips the `libapp.a in Resources` pbxproj entry. Sibling of [[project_ios_framework_linking]] Patch E.
- **base64 shim** (`ios-env.sh`, gated on `EZPDS_IOS_BUILD`): Nix's GNU `base64` shadows macOS BSD `base64`, but Tauri's cert decode uses BSD `-i/-o` flags → `invalid option -- 'o'`. Shim prefers `/usr/bin/base64`. Local-only (no-op on CI).
- **`src-tauri/Info.ios.plist`** (Tauri merges it LAST, after the plugin's build.rs): carries `ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption=false` (export-compliance — auto-clears TestFlight "Missing Compliance") AND `CFBundleURLTypes` registering the `dev.malpercio.identitywallet` custom scheme for the OAuth deep-link callback. tauri-plugin-deep-link 2.4.7 can't register pure custom schemes for iOS (it *removes* `CFBundleURLTypes` unless an entry is a valid https app-link), so this plist IS the registration — without it iOS can't open the app on the OAuth redirect ("could not be opened").
